key_insight: QVal argues that dense supervision signals for long-horizon LLM agents should be evaluated cheaply and directly, rather than only by expensive downstream task performance. It introduces a practical way to compare intermediate-step scoring methods so practitioners can tell which signals are actually useful.
problem_solved: Long-horizon LLM agents produce very long trajectories, making outcome-only rewards too sparse to guide learning. Existing dense supervision methods are hard to evaluate fairly because their quality is usually judged only through costly downstream experiments.
method: Proposes a cheap evaluation framework for dense supervision signals used in long-horizon agent trajectories.
Measures how well intermediate-step scores reflect action quality, instead of relying only on end-task success.
Supports comparison across common dense supervision sources such as confidence-based scores, self-distillation, and embedding similarity signals.
impact: This helps researchers and engineers select better training or evaluation signals without running full-scale downstream experiments every time. It can speed up development of more effective long-horizon agents and reduce evaluation cost.
visual_elements: Long trajectory timeline showing sparse outcome reward versus dense intermediate scores
Side-by-side comparison chart of different dense supervision methods
Flow diagram of agent actions -> step scores -> evaluation -> downstream performance
Icon set for confidence, embeddings, and self-distillation signals
paper_title: QVal: Cheaply Evaluating Dense Supervision Signals for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
paper_authors: Sergio Hernández-Gutiérrez, Matteo Merler, Ilze Amanda Auzina, Joschka Strüber, Ameya Prabhu
